Very common in the first days. A newborn's circulation is still settling, so hands and feet can look bluish or purple, especially when cold, while the lips, tongue and face stay pink.
Call {sos} if the lips, tongue or face look blue or grey, or your baby is struggling to breathe.

A soft bulge at the belly button that gets bigger when crying is usually an umbilical hernia. It often closes on its own in the first years. A ridge down the middle of the tummy when straining is the belly muscles not yet joined (diastasis recti) and usually goes away as your baby grows.
Call your pediatrician straight away if a bulge is hard, tender or discoloured, can't be gently pushed back, or comes with vomiting.
Soft clicks from knees, shoulders and hips are common as ligaments stretch. Doctors check the hips at every early checkup.
Mention it at the next visit if you feel a "clunk" in a hip, the skin folds on the thighs look uneven, the legs look different lengths, or one leg moves less.
Mild yellowing of the skin and eyes is common between days 2 and 5 and usually fades within two weeks. Frequent feeds help.

Call if yellow appears in the first 24 hours, spreads to the belly, arms or legs, lasts more than two weeks, or your baby is very sleepy or feeding poorly. Pale or chalky poop or dark urine also needs a call.
Keep it clean and dry and let it fall off by itself, usually in 1 to 3 weeks. A little crust or a spot of blood when it comes off is normal.
Call if the skin around it turns red, there is pus or a bad smell, bleeding doesn't stop with gentle pressure, or your baby has a fever.
Most babies spit up, often after feeds or with burps. If your baby is growing and content, it is usually just "laundry".
Call if vomiting is forceful or projectile (especially between 2 and 8 weeks), contains blood, or your baby has fewer wet diapers. Green vomit needs a doctor straight away.

strings.note: Guide topic: what the colours of a baby's poo mean.

strings.en: The first poops are black and sticky (meconium), then green, then yellow and seedy for breastfed babies or tan and firmer with formula. How often varies a lot.
Call about white, pale grey or chalky poop, red or bloody poop, or black poop after the first few days.
Expect about one wet diaper per day of age for the first few days, then at least 6 wet diapers a day from about day 5.
Call if there are fewer than 6 wet diapers a day after the first week, a dry diaper for 6 hours or more, or a sunken soft spot.
Sneezing, snuffly noses, hiccups and breathing that speeds up and slows down with short pauses (under about 10 seconds) are normal in newborns.
Call {sos} for pauses of 20 seconds or more, blue colour, or hard work to breathe: skin pulling in between the ribs, flaring nostrils, or grunting with every breath.
Take the temperature rectally for an accurate reading in young babies. A fever is 100.4°F (38°C) or higher.
Under 3 months, any fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher means calling your pediatrician or going to the emergency room now, even if your baby seems well.
Tiny white bumps (milia), baby acne, blotchy red newborn rash, dry peeling skin and cradle cap are common and harmless. Gentle washing is all they need.
Call about blisters, pus-filled spots, a rash with a fever, or purple-red spots that don't fade when pressed.

Crying usually peaks around 6 weeks and eases by 3 to 4 months. Colic is crying for 3 hours or more a day, on 3 or more days a week, in a healthy baby. Swaddling, rocking, white noise and walks can help.
Never shake a baby. If you feel overwhelmed, put your baby down safely on their back and take a break. Call if the cry sounds unusual or high-pitched, or comes with fever, vomiting or poor feeding.
Startles, jerks and a trembling chin
The startle (Moro) reflex, jerky arm movements and a quivering chin are normal as the nervous system matures.
Call if there is rhythmic jerking that doesn't stop when you gently hold the limb, or jerking with staring or not responding.
Eyes that cross or drift now and then are common in the first months while the eye muscles strengthen.
Mention it if an eye turns in or out all the time, or still wanders after about 4 months.
Hormones from pregnancy can cause swollen breasts (even a little milky fluid) and swollen genitals. Baby girls may have a little white or blood-tinged discharge. It settles in a few weeks.
Call if a breast is red, hot or tender.
Losing some weight (up to about 7 to 10%) in the first days is normal. Most babies are back to birth weight by 10 to 14 days.
Call if your baby isn't feeding well, seems weak or very sleepy, or the scale at checkups is worrying.
Every sleep: on the back, on a firm flat mattress, in their own crib or bassinet in your room, with nothing else in it. No pillows, bumpers, blankets or soft toys, and never on a couch or armchair.

Cradle cap: greasy, yellowish scales on the scalp. Harmless and not itchy. Washing the hair and gently loosening the scales with a soft brush helps; don't pick them off.
A baby whose face, chest and belly look yellow.

Jaundice: the skin and the whites of the eyes look yellow. This baby was 6 weeks old. Jaundice lasting more than two weeks needs a check; here it came from an underactive thyroid, which treatment put right. On brown or black skin, look for yellow in the whites of the eyes, the gums, palms and soles.

Jaundice shows first on the face and moves down the body as it gets stronger (zones I to V). Call if it spreads to the belly, arms or legs. To check, press gently on the forehead or nose in daylight: skin that looks yellow where you pressed means jaundice.

A bigger one. Soft hernias that go back in when the baby is calm are common and usually close by themselves; call straight away if one turns hard, tender or discoloured.

Most children are ready between about 18 months and 3 years. Signs: staying dry for about 2 hours, telling you about a wet or dirty diaper, being curious about the toilet, and pulling pants up and down. Keep it relaxed: praise every try, expect accidents, and never punish. Staying dry at night often comes months or years later; wetting the bed is common until about 5, and later in some children.
Talk to your pediatrician if peeing or pooing hurts, or if a child who was dry starts having accidents again.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide: toddlers who refuse foods or eat little.

strings.en: Toddlers grow more slowly than babies, so they often eat less and refuse new foods. Offer three meals and two or three snacks at regular times, put one food they like next to each new one, and let them decide how much to eat. It can take 10 or more tries before a new food is accepted. Milk: about 2 cups (500 ml) a day at most, to leave room for food.
Choking risks under 4: whole grapes, nuts, popcorn, hard sweets and round slices of sausage. Cut round foods into quarters, and stay with them while they eat.

Tantrums are normal between about 1 and 3 years, when feelings are big and words are few. Keep your child safe, stay calm and close, and let it pass; name the feeling afterwards ("You were angry"). Being tired or hungry makes them more likely, so routines help. Praise the times they cope.
Talk to your pediatrician if tantrums are very frequent or long, if your child hurts themselves or others, or if they are still frequent after 4.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide: how much toddlers sleep, naps, moving to a bed.

strings.en: Children of 1 to 2 need 11 to 14 hours of sleep in 24 hours, naps included, and 3 to 5 year olds 10 to 13. Most go down to one nap between 15 and 18 months and stop napping between 3 and 5. A calm bedtime routine at the same time every night helps. Move to a bed when they start climbing out of the crib, usually between 2 and 3½.

Brush twice a day: a smear of fluoride toothpaste the size of a grain of rice until 3, then a pea-sized amount. See a dentist when the first tooth comes or by the first birthday, then about every 6 months. Water and milk are the best drinks, and no bottle in bed.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide: screen time (phones, tablets, TV).

strings.en: Under 18 months, no screens apart from video calls. From 18 months to 2 years, a little good content watched together. From 2 to 5, up to an hour a day of good programmes, ideally with you. Keep screens out of the bedroom and off for an hour before bed.

Keep your child rear-facing for as long as the seat allows: it protects the head and neck best. Then a forward-facing seat with a harness, then a booster seat until the adult seat belt fits, usually between 8 and 12 years. Check the seat's limits and the rules where you live.

Vaccines protect children from serious illnesses, and work best on time, following your country's schedule: your doctor, nurse or health visitor has it. A sore, red spot where the needle went in, a mild fever, or a fussy or sleepy day or two are common afterwards. Keep each dose in the health record.

Call {sos} straight away for trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or a child who is floppy or hard to wake after a vaccine. Call your doctor for a fever of 40°C (104°F) or more, crying for 3 hours or more, or anything that worries you.

Regular checkups follow how your child grows and develops, check their hearing and eyes, and give the vaccines that are due. There are several in the first year, and they get further apart after that. In the US they are usually at 3 to 5 days, 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 24 and 30 months, then every year from 3; other countries have their own. The dentist every 6 months from the first tooth. Write your questions down before you go.

Each measurement is compared with children of the same age and sex. The 50th percentile is the middle: half of children are smaller and half are bigger. Anywhere from the 3rd to the 97th is usual. What matters most is that your child keeps growing along their own line. The app uses the CDC growth charts; your doctor may use another, such as the WHO's.
Talk to your doctor if your child crosses two of the lines on the chart, stops growing, or loses weight.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Children of 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night. A regular bedtime, at weekends too, and an hour to wind down without screens help. A tired child can seem restless, moody or unable to focus rather than sleepy. Tell your doctor about loud snoring most nights or pauses in breathing while asleep.

Agree on screen time together, so it doesn't crowd out sleep, homework, play and family meals, and keep devices out of the bedroom at night. Know the apps and games they use and set up parental controls. Teach them never to share personal details or photos, never to meet someone they only know online, and to tell you about anything that upsets them.

Reading together, or listening to them read, for 10 to 20 minutes most days helps more than anything else. Give homework a regular time and a quiet place, with you nearby but not doing it for them, and praise the effort more than the marks. If reading, writing or numbers are much harder for them than for their classmates, or they dread school, talk to the teacher.

Friends matter more and more at this age: ask about their day, their friends and break times. Not wanting to go to school, lost or broken things, unexplained bruises, poor sleep or a change in mood can be signs of bullying. Listen calmly, tell them it isn't their fault, and talk to the school together.

Breakfast every day, three meals and one or two healthy snacks, water or milk rather than sugary drinks, and fruit or vegetables at every meal. Children need at least 60 minutes of activity a day that gets them out of breath: running, cycling, swimming, sports or active play.

Brush twice a day with a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste, and keep helping or checking until they brush well on their own, often at 7 or 8. Baby teeth start to fall out at about 6, and the first adult back teeth come in behind them: ask the dentist about sealants. A mouthguard for contact sports.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide: wetting the bed at night.

strings.en: Wetting the bed is common in young children, often runs in the family, and isn't their fault: they can't help it. A waterproof cover, the toilet before bed and no blame or punishment help most. Most children grow out of it.

Talk to your doctor if it still happens often after 7 or upsets your child, if a child who had been dry for months starts wetting again, or if there is pain when peeing, a fever, or wetting in the day.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide: a child's worries, anxiety and mood.

strings.en: Worries are part of growing up. Look out for changes that last more than a couple of weeks: trouble sleeping, tummy aches before school, losing interest in friends or things they enjoyed, or being unusually tearful or angry. Make time to listen without rushing to fix it, and talk to your doctor if it goes on or gets in the way of school, friends or sleep.
If your child talks about hurting themselves or not wanting to be alive, take it seriously: stay with them and call your doctor or {sos} now.

Puberty usually starts between 8 and 13 in girls (breasts start to grow first) and between 9 and 14 in boys (the testicles get bigger first). Talk about the changes before they happen: periods, wet dreams, body hair, spots, body odour and feelings.
Talk to your doctor if the signs start before 8 in a girl or 9 in a boy, or haven't started by 13 in a girl or 14 in a boy.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Head lice are common in school children and have nothing to do with being clean. To check, comb wet hair with conditioner and a fine-toothed detection comb. Treat only when you find a live louse: wet combing every few days for 2 weeks, or a treatment from the pharmacy, and check everyone at home.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide for school children: safety on bikes and scooters, in the car, near water and crossing roads.

strings.en: A helmet on bikes and scooters. A booster seat until the adult seat belt fits, usually between 8 and 12 years. Swimming lessons, and an adult watching near water. Practise crossing roads together: most children can't judge traffic safely on their own until about 10.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep. Their body clock moves later, so they feel awake at night and tired in the morning: a regular wake-up time, at weekends too, helps, and so does daylight in the morning. Phones and screens out of the bedroom at night make the biggest difference.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Moods swing in the teenage years, but sadness, worry, anger or withdrawal that lasts more than two weeks, falling marks, sleeping or eating much more or less, or self-harm (cuts, burns) need help. Ask how they are, listen without judging, and see your doctor together.
If your teenager talks about suicide or hurting themselves, take it seriously: stay with them, remove anything they could use to hurt themselves, and call {sos} or a crisis line now.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Agree on the rules together: no phones at meals or at night, and time for sleep, homework and friends. Talk about what they see online, about privacy and about photos: once sent, a picture can be shared. Tell them they can always come to you, without blame, if anything goes wrong or someone threatens them.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Talk early and often, with facts rather than scare stories, and say what you expect. The teenage brain is still growing and is more easily harmed by alcohol, nicotine and cannabis. Offer a lift home at any hour, with no questions that night.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Talk about respect and consent in friendships and relationships, about contraception and sexually transmitted infections, and about where they can get confidential advice and care. Teenagers who can talk to their parents tend to start later and stay safer. The HPV vaccine protects against several cancers.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide: menstruation.

strings.en: Periods usually start at around 12, about two years after the breasts start to grow, but anywhere from 8 to 16 can be normal. Talk about them before they begin, and keep pads or period underwear ready.
Talk to your doctor if periods haven't started by 15, or if they are very heavy, very painful, or keep your teenager off school.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Spots are common from puberty. Wash gently twice a day, don't squeeze, and try a pharmacy cream with benzoyl peroxide. See your doctor if acne is severe, leaves scars or upsets your teenager: there are treatments that work.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Regular meals, breakfast included, and an hour of activity a day. Notice comments about weight, skipped meals, a lot of exercise, or weight lost fast: eating disorders are easier to treat early, so see your doctor if you are worried.
After a knock to the head in sport, stop playing if there is a headache, dizziness, confusion or vomiting, and see a doctor the same day. Call {sos} if they pass out, have a seizure or keep vomiting.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: New drivers have the most crashes in their first year. Practise together in all kinds of weather, agree on rules (no phone, no alcohol, a seat belt on every trip, few friends in the car at first), and keep wearing a helmet on bikes and scooters.

strings.note: A topic of the Guide.

strings.en: Give them more say and more to do: their own money, cooking, booking their own appointments and seeing the doctor on their own for part of the visit. Respect their privacy while keeping them safe, and keep talking: at dinner, in the car, late at night.

Puberty: what to expect and when

Puberty usually starts between 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys, and takes a few years. In girls the breasts grow first, then hair under the arms and between the legs, a growth spurt, and periods about two years after the breasts started. In boys the testicles grow first, then hair, a deeper voice, a growth spurt later than the girls' and sometimes tender breast tissue for a while, which goes. Everyone sweats more, gets oilier skin and hair, spots, and bigger feelings: moods, tiredness, wanting to be left alone. All of it is normal, and so is being early or late compared with friends.
See your doctor if signs of puberty start before 8 in a girl or 9 in a boy, or if there are none by 13 in a girl or 14 in a boy.

Start before it starts, in small everyday conversations rather than one big talk: in the car, cooking, walking. Use the real words for body parts, say what will change and that it happens to everyone, and answer what is asked without adding a lecture. Books written for their age help, and so does a parent or relative of the same sex when they would rather ask them. Deodorant, a shower every day, a bra when they want one, pads or period underwear in their bag before the first period, a razor only if they ask: let them lead on what they are ready for.

From now on, some things are theirs to share. Knock before going into their room, keep what they tell you between you unless someone is in danger, and from about 12 let them see the doctor on their own for part of a visit. Little Log is shared with everyone in the family: ask before writing anything here about their body, periods or feelings, and leave it out if they would rather. Health notes are seen by everyone with health access, and the Day page by every helper.

Newborns play with their eyes and ears. They see best about 8 to 12 inches (20 to 30 cm) away and like strong contrast, faces and slow movement. The best toy is you: your face, your voice, and a little tummy time every day.

Nothing goes in the crib for sleep: no soft toys, pillows, bumpers or loose blankets until 1 year. No cords, ribbons or strings within reach, and a mobile comes down once the baby can push up on hands and knees.

From about 3 months babies reach, grab and put everything in their mouths; from 6 they sit up and pass things from hand to hand; from 9 they crawl, point and drop things on purpose to see what happens. Toys that do something when they act (a sound, a pop-up, a roll) teach cause and effect.

Anything that fits through a toilet-paper tube can choke a baby: check for small parts, loose eyes and button batteries, and keep older children's toys apart. Skip baby walkers (the AAP has called for a ban: falls down stairs), and keep bouncers and jumpers to 15 to 20 minutes.

Toddlers walk, climb, carry and empty everything, and begin to pretend. Open-ended toys (blocks, boxes, a doll, a toy kitchen) keep their interest far longer than a toy that does one thing; add something to push or ride and something to scribble with.

Keep checking for small parts until 3 (nothing that fits through a toilet-paper tube), and keep magnets and button batteries well away: swallowed, they can do serious harm within hours. A helmet on any ride-on outdoors, and anchor furniture and TVs a climber could pull over.

Preschoolers build, draw, dress up and play together, with longer stories and first rules. Toys for making things and acting out roles grow with them; this is also the age for a bike (a balance bike first, then pedals) and for games with simple turns.

A helmet on anything with wheels, every time. Trampolines, above all with more than one child on them, cause many broken bones: if you have one, one child at a time and a net. Keep screens mostly to shows watched together, and out of the bedroom.

School children want to get good at things: a sport, a craft, a game with real rules, a collection. Hobbies that take practice beat gadgets that do it for them, and the best toys get them moving, making, or playing with other children.

Helmets stay on for bikes, scooters and skates, and wrist guards for skates. Keep magnets, chemistry sets and anything that shoots small projectiles away from younger brothers and sisters. For video games, check the age rating, play some together, and agree time limits before the console arrives.

Teenagers play through hobbies, sport, music, games and friends. A gift that feeds a real interest (gear for their sport, an instrument, an art or electronics kit, a game to play together) means more than the latest gadget, and games played as a family are a good way to stay close.
Gear for the sport they chose, or a gym or pool pass
Strategy board games, card games and puzzles to play as a family
Craft, electronics, coding or robotics kits
Books they choose themselves, or a bookshop voucher
A bike or skateboard (with a helmet), a camera, a journal

Helmets still matter: head injuries peak in the teenage years. Talk about the age ratings, chat features and in-game spending of the games they play, and let phones and consoles charge outside the bedroom at night.

Babies can enjoy the water with you from a few months old (a warm pool, short sessions, you holding them), and parent-and-baby classes build water confidence, not safety. The AAP says swim lessons can begin around age 1, when they lower a toddler's risk of drowning, and that most children are ready for formal lessons by 4; some countries' programmes start water familiarisation from 6 months. Look for small groups, a warm pool and teachers trained in water safety and CPR, and keep going until your child can float, tread water, swim a length and climb out on their own.

In many countries drowning is the leading cause of death for children of 1 to 4, and it is silent and quick. Stay within arm's reach of a child under 5 near any water, fence pools on all four sides, empty paddling pools and buckets after use, and put life jackets on at the lake or on a boat. Lessons never replace watching.

The school years: friends, learning and growing independence. Children of 6 to 12 need 9 to 12 hours of sleep and at least an hour of active play a day. A yearly checkup, the dentist every 6 months, and the vaccines on your country's schedule.

The teenage years: growing fast, more independence, and big changes in body and mood. Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep and at least an hour of activity a day. A yearly checkup, the dentist every 6 months, and the vaccines due on your country's schedule. Talk openly, and give them more say as they grow.

Breastfed and partly breastfed babies need vitamin D every day: 400 IU in the US, 8.5 to 10 micrograms in the UK. Babies having more than about 500 ml of formula a day get enough from the formula in the UK; in the US, ask your pediatrician.

Many parents tell of good results with these. Studies haven't found homeopathic remedies to work better than a placebo, and they aren't tested for safety and strength the way medicines are. Treat them as optional extras, tell your pediatrician, and never use one instead of seeing a doctor when your baby is unwell.
